newsitem.title: UK: Blair woos UK business with offer to work together.
newsitem.headline: Blair woos UK business with offer to work together.

text.p: Opposition Labour leader Tony Blair on Tuesday opened up a new front in his push for power, courting British business with a pledge not to scrap the radical free-market reforms introduced by the ruling Conservative party.

Keeping up pressure on the government a day after the Labour Party boldly promised not to raise taxes if it won the coming election, Blair assured businessmen that he wanted to forge a new alliance with them to boost Britain's economic performance.

"Today I offer business a new deal for the future. The deal is this: we leave intact the main changes of the 1980s in industrial relations and enterprise. And now, together, we address a new agenda for the 21st century -- education, welfare reform, infrastructure, leadership in Europe," Blair said.

The pro-business pitch and the no-tax pledge are the latest examples of how Blair has dramatically shifted Labour from the left of British politics to centre-right territory that has hitherto been the exclusive preserve of the Conservatives.
The Labour Party are strong opinion poll favourites to win the election that Prime Minister John Major must call by May 22.
The ruling party wasted no time in attacking the forum that provided Blair with his platform -- the left-leaning Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank.

Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said a report the IPPR had commissioned from a group of businessmen and academics, which largely endorsed Labour's policies, was seriously flawed and did not do justice to the government's economic record.
"I must in honesty go further. I question the motives of those who cloak their political intentions with academic respectability," Heseltine said.
Blair said Labour, in opposition since 1979, would not be ruled by dogma or doctrine in its search for the policies needed to make Britain more competitive.
He said the government's drive to deregulate and privatise British industry, begun under former prime minister Margaret Thatcher, had largely run its course.
But he said Labour wanted to keep the Conservatives' flexible labour market laws -- despite the loss of influence they have meant for Labour's traditional trade union allies.
"The serious task of an incoming Labour government is not to alter what is working, but to put right what isn't," Blair, whose party enjoys a handsome lead in opinion polls, said.

He said Labour would raise Britain's competitiveness by ensuring economic stability, boosting education and skills, reforming the welfare state, tempering labour market flexibilty with fairness and overhauling the country's competition laws.
Blair plans more high-profile meetings with executives in the run-up to the election to underscore his claim that Labour is now a natural ally of business.
